    In plain words

    A serious flaw in WordPress, software used to run websites, is being actively used by attackers, according to the U.S. cyber agency CISA. The weakness can let someone without a site account run their own code on a website’s server during the short period when WordPress is being fully updated. Security researchers have already seen thousands of attempts, so website owners need to install the available fix; U.S. federal agencies must do so by November 6, 2026.

    Summary
    CISA has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-119977, a high-severity unauthenticated WordPress Core race condition that can enable remote code execution during full-package updates. Organizations should apply the available patches immediately, with U.S. federal agencies required to remediate by November 6, 2026.

    CISA has added CVE-2026-119977, a high-severity WordPress Core issue with a CVSS score of 8.1, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after confirming active exploitation. The flaw is a time-of-check/time-of-use race condition that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on an affected server. Patches were released late last month. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must apply fixes by November 6, 2026.

    The issue occurs during the brief window of a complete WordPress Core update and is tied to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used in full-package upgrades. Attackers can target staged setup-config.php installer paths without needing an account on the site. Wordfence recorded more than 18,500 related requests in the first 21 hours after public disclosure and said it blocked 12,632 attempted attacks in the most recent 24-hour period. Previdian also recorded three attempts against its honeypot sensors from an IP address geolocated in the U.K. on October 30, 2026.

    • The attack does not require an account on the targeted WordPress site, but it depends on exploiting a short opportunity that exists while a complete WordPress Core update is underway.
    • Attack activity appeared rapidly after disclosure: Wordfence saw more than 18,500 requests targeting the relevant staged installer paths within the first 21 hours.
    • CISA’s confirmation of active exploitation makes remediation time-bound for U.S. federal civilian agencies, which must apply fixes by November 6, 2026.

In plain words

U.S. cybersecurity officials say attackers are actively using a recently fixed weakness in WordPress, the software that powers many websites. During a website update, the flaw can let an outsider run their own commands on the site’s server, potentially taking control of it. U.S. federal agencies must fix affected systems by Friday, and other organizations are also urged to install WordPress 7.1.4 quickly because thousands of attempts to abuse the issue were blocked in a single day.

Summary
CISA has added the actively exploited WordPress Core flaw CVE-2026-119977 to its KEV catalog after attackers began targeting the upgrade-process race condition, which can enable remote code execution during full-package updates. Organizations should update to WordPress 7.1.4 immediately.

CISA has warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-119977, a recently patched high-severity vulnerability in WordPress Core. The agency added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and directed U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure affected systems by Friday under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. CISA also urged private-sector defenders to prioritize remediation.

The issue is a time-of-check/time-of-use race condition in WordPress’s upgrade process. During full-package core upgrades, predictable, web-accessible staging paths can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on the server in a high-complexity attack. WordPress released version 7.1.4 with fixes on October 28 and recommended that site owners update immediately.

Wordfence said it blocked 13,095 attacks targeting CVE-2026-119977 during the preceding 24 hours. The article also notes earlier WordPress Core wp2shell flaws that received public exploits shortly after patches were released and were subsequently used to install webshells and malicious plugins on unpatched servers. A Chinese-speaking threat actor later used that earlier exploit chain to steal data from backend databases belonging to small businesses and government organizations.

  • The vulnerable condition occurs specifically during full-package WordPress core upgrades, meaning the exposure is tied to an update window rather than ordinary day-to-day site use.
  • Attackers do not need prior privileges to exploit the flaw, although the article describes the attack as high-complexity.
  • Wordfence said it blocked 13,095 attempts targeting this issue in 24 hours, indicating that exploitation activity was already occurring at substantial volume after CISA’s warning.
  • The article notes that public exploits for the earlier wp2shell WordPress flaws appeared one day after patches were released and were followed by compromises within days, highlighting the urgency of applying WordPress security updates.
Key Points
  • 01CISA added the actively exploited high-severity WordPress Core vulnerability CVE-2026-119977 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog.
  • 02The flaw is a race condition in the WordPress upgrade process that can allow unauthenticated remote attackers to execute code on a server during full-package core upgrades.
  • 03WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28 with patches for CVE-2026-119977 and recommended that sites update immediately.
  • 04CISA ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure affected systems by Friday under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.
  • 05Wordfence reported blocking 13,095 attacks targeting CVE-2026-119977 in the preceding 24 hours.

    bleepingcomputer.com · 04 Nov 2026 09:39 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra

    In plain words

    Researchers say a Russian-linked group used hacked websites and convincing copycat sites to quietly target people using iPhones and Android phones. Simply visiting one of these sites could let the attackers identify the visitor’s phone and browser, then steal information such as website logins, browser cookies, photos, location data, and WhatsApp or Telegram data. The affected sites included organizations in the United States, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria, and a compromised website-tracking service exposed visitors to thousands of sites, mainly in Ukraine. Apple and Google have fixed the weaknesses used, so installing the latest phone and browser updates is important.

    Summary
    A suspected APT29 watering-hole campaign used compromised and impersonated websites to fingerprint iOS and Android visitors, then silently deliver device-specific n-day exploit chains that stole cookies, credentials, messaging data, and other sensitive information. Apple and Google have patched the exploited flaws, so users should install the latest available updates.

    Sekoia says a large-scale watering-hole campaign linked with moderate-to-high confidence to Russian threat group APT29, also known as Midnight Blizzard, targeted iOS and Android users. The attackers used compromised legitimate sites, fake sites impersonating America250 and Raffles London at The OWO, and a compromised Plerdy SEO tracker that was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine. Affected infrastructure and sites were connected to the United States, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria.

    Injected JavaScript profiled visitors’ devices and browser versions, after which a command-and-control server delivered a platform-specific exploit chain without requiring user interaction. The chains exploited known flaws in iOS and Chrome for Android to steal data including cookies, credentials, WhatsApp and Telegram databases, photos, location information, browsing history, and saved Wi-Fi credentials. Sekoia found that the analyzed payloads did not establish persistence, so rebooting stops the malicious activity until the user visits a compromised site again; Apple and Google have patched all identified flaws and users are advised to apply the latest security updates.

    • The attackers first profiled each visitor’s device and browser version, allowing them to select an exploit chain tailored to that visitor rather than sending the same payload to everyone.
    • Compromising Plerdy’s SEO tracker created a supply-chain-like distribution path because the modified tracker was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine, between August 27 and September 3.
    • The iOS 18.5 chain was capable of reaching beyond browser data to collect WhatsApp and Telegram databases, Keychain credentials, location data, and photos.
    • The analyzed payloads did not maintain access after infection, meaning a reboot stopped their activity unless the person later visited a compromised site again.
    • The campaign relied on already known flaws rather than undisclosed ones, and Apple and Google have released patches for every vulnerability identified in the active exploit chains.
    Key Points
    • 01Sekoia attributed a large-scale watering-hole campaign with moderate-to-high confidence to APT29, also known as Midnight Blizzard, a Russian threat group.
    • 02The campaign used compromised legitimate websites, impersonated sites, and a compromised Plerdy web analytics service to profile iOS and Android visitors and deliver device-specific exploit chains without user interaction.
    • 03The exploit chains targeted iOS 16.7 and iOS 18.5 devices as well as Chrome for Android versions 139 through 145, excluding version 143.
    • 04The payloads could collect Safari or Chrome cookies, credentials, messaging-app databases, photos, location data, browsing history, and saved Wi-Fi credentials.
    • 05Apple and Google have patched all of the flaws used in the campaign, and Sekoia said the analyzed payloads did not establish persistence, so rebooting stops the malicious activity until a victim revisits a compromised site.

In plain words

A Russia-linked hacking group called APT29 reportedly placed harmful code on legitimate websites, fake lookalike sites, and a Ukrainian website-analytics service, so it could target people using iPhones and Android phones. Simply visiting one of these pages could lead to theft of browser information, saved Wi-Fi passwords, and, on some iPhones, highly personal data such as messages, photos, contacts, call history, and app data. The affected sites include organizations connected to chemical industry, politics, military matters, and the Russia-Ukraine war, suggesting that some visitors may have been especially valuable targets. This matters because people may be exposed without downloading anything or clicking a suspicious link if their phone software is not up to date.

Summary
APT29-linked operators compromised websites, lookalike domains, and Plerdy’s analytics script to silently deliver DarkSword iOS and AndroSnitch Android exploit chains to visitors. The campaign can steal browser data, Wi‑Fi credentials, and—in some iOS cases—extensive device data, underscoring the risk of unpatched mobile browsers and operating systems.

Sekoia said the Russia-linked APT29 group conducted a large watering-hole campaign, dubbed Poisoned Source, against iOS and Android users. The group reportedly compromised legitimate websites, created lookalike sites, and inserted malicious code into Plerdy SEO Tracker’s JavaScript file between August 27 and September 3, 2026. The malicious script collected browser and device details, then directed visitors to a platform-specific exploit chain.

On iOS, the campaign used DarkSword to steal browser cookies and, for some iOS 18.5 targets, collect extensive device data including messages, contacts, photos, call history, Wi-Fi passwords, and data from Apple applications and services. On Android, exploits for Chrome versions 139 through 145 delivered AndroSnitch, which collected Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without persistence. The article also describes related Coruna and DarkSword distribution campaigns that use malicious advertisements, expired analytics and advertising domains, lure sites, and compromised websites to target iPhone users simply by having them open a vulnerable web page.

  • The compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026 turned a widely loaded web analytics script into a distribution route affecting visitors to high-value military and defense-related websites.
  • The Android exploit chain specifically stopped when it detected a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra model identifier, an unusual device-selection condition noted by the researchers.
  • DeadTag operators used more than 660 expired domains associated with old analytics and advertising tags that were still being loaded by thousands of websites, allowing malicious code to reach visitors through forgotten web dependencies.
  • The DeadTag delivery scripts reportedly withheld content from search engines, security scanners, automated browsers, and other visitors that appeared to be bots, making the activity less visible to automated inspection.
  • Sekoia said the reuse of packaged N-day mobile exploit chains such as DarkSword lowers the cost and technical threshold for state-sponsored groups to conduct advanced mobile compromise.
Key Points
  • 01Sekoia attributed the Poisoned Source watering-hole campaign to the Russia-linked APT29 group and said it targeted iOS and Android users through compromised sites, lookalike domains, and a compromised Plerdy SEO Tracker script.
  • 02The injected JavaScript profiled visitors’ browsers and devices before delivering platform-specific exploit chains for iOS or Android.
  • 03The iOS DarkSword chain could steal browser cookies or, for some iOS 18.5 devices, collect extensive data including messages, contacts, photos, call history, Wi-Fi passwords, and data from several Apple services and apps.
  • 04The Android chain used CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to deliver AndroSnitch, which collected Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence.
  • 05Researchers also reported that Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits were being distributed through malicious advertising, expired web-tag domains, lure sites, and compromised legitimate websites.

Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick Uploads
thehackernews.com · 04 Nov 2026 12:07 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSactive-storagecve-2026-66066debianffmpegghsa-f3w6-w445-fwh9ghsa-v924-7rp8-4mxhgmo-flatt-securitygraphicsmagickimagemagickminimagickmslruby-on-railsubuntu
94
In plain words

Ruby on Rails disclosed a serious flaw that can let an unauthenticated person upload a specially made image file and cause a website’s server to write files where it should not. It affects Rails apps that accept untrusted uploads, use ImageMagick to handle images, and have not already blocked the risky image-processing features. If the app saves uploads on its own server, an attacker may also be able to read secret keys and service passwords, potentially taking over the app or reaching other connected systems. Site owners should install the fixed Rails releases and replace any secrets that may have been exposed.

Summary
Rails apps using Active Storage with ImageMagick may let unauthenticated attackers write arbitrary server files—and, with Disk storage, read secrets—through crafted uploads. Upgrade to Rails 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2, ensure MiniMagick 5.1+ and the new ImageMagick policy are active, and rotate potentially exposed secrets.

Ruby on Rails disclosed a critical Active Storage flaw that can let an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on a server by uploading a crafted file when the application processes uploads with ImageMagick. The issue is rated 9.8 out of 10, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9, and was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK of GMO Flatt Security. Rails fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

The vulnerable path occurs when Active Storage analyzes an attached upload, so an application does not need to create an image variant, preview, or explicitly call analysis for the flaw to be reached. An uploaded SVG can reach ImageMagick’s MSL coder, which can read and write files named in its script. Applications are affected when they accept untrusted uploads, use MiniMagick for Active Storage processing, and do not already have an ImageMagick policy blocking the relevant coders.

Apps using Active Storage’s Disk service may also permit reading files available to the application, including secret_key_base and credentials, which Rails says may lead to remote code execution or movement into connected systems. Rails recommends upgrading, confirming that its shipped ImageMagick policy is loaded, and checking that existing policy rules do not override its protections. For Disk-service applications, Rails also advises rotating all secrets the application process could read, including master keys, database and storage credentials, and third-party tokens.

  • Simply attaching a crafted upload can trigger the vulnerable ImageMagick analysis path; the application does not need to create an image thumbnail or preview first.
  • The Rails-supplied ImageMagick policy may not protect an app if it replaces MiniMagick.cli_env after startup, clears its environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or uses its own MiniMagick::Shell.
  • A permissive rule in the server’s existing ImageMagick policy, including a wildcard that allows all handlers, can override the new Rails policy’s blocks.
  • Applications using GraphicsMagick do not receive protection from Rails’ shipped ImageMagick policy because GraphicsMagick does not load ImageMagick policies.
  • For apps using on-server Disk storage, applying the patch alone is insufficient if exposure occurred; Rails advises rotating every secret the application process could read.
Key Points
  • 01Ruby on Rails disclosed a critical Active Storage flaw that can allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files through crafted uploads processed by ImageMagick.
  • 02Applications using Active Storage’s Disk service may also allow attackers to read files accessible to the application process, including secret_key_base and credentials.
  • 03The issue affects applications that accept untrusted uploads, use MiniMagick for Active Storage image processing, and do not have an ImageMagick policy that blocks the relevant file handlers.
  • 04Rails fixed the flaw in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2 by shipping an ImageMagick security policy that blocks the MSL handler and other risky functionality.
  • 05Rails recommends affected users upgrade promptly, confirm the new policy is loaded, and rotate secrets accessible to apps using the Disk service.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a critical Rails Active Storage patch for a flaw rated CVSS 9.8 that can enable unauthenticated arbitrary file writes through crafted uploads, with potential secret disclosure for apps using Disk storage. It affects applications accepting untrusted uploads with MiniMagick/ImageMagick and requires prompt upgrading, policy validation, and potentially secret rotation.

In plain words

Zyxel fixed a newly discovered security weakness in its GS1900 network switches, devices that help connect computers and other equipment on a network. Hackers had already used the flaw to take control of nearly 1,000 switches in 48 countries and copy device settings, password data, and network details. The issue matters because an earlier Zyxel update did not stop this separate weakness, so organizations using these switches need the latest update to prevent unauthorized access to their networks.

Summary
Zyxel patched CVE-2026-107441, an actively exploited unauthenticated remote-code-execution zero-day in GS1900 network switches that attackers used to compromise nearly 1,000 devices and steal configurations and credentials. Administrators should install the October 22 firmware updates, as earlier patches for CVE-2026-7273 did not stop this separate flaw.

Zyxel released firmware updates for CVE-2026-107441, an actively exploited zero-day affecting ten GS1900 network switch models. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write issue in the switches’ web management interface that lets an unauthenticated person with network access run operating-system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. GreyNoise observed the Kapibala threat actor compromise 996 devices in 48 countries, collecting device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information.

The activity was initially attributed to CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication buffer overflow flaw Zyxel patched in June, and CISA added that CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Binarly’s analysis of a recovered exploit found it was actually targeting a separate, previously unknown issue and remained effective against all ten firmware releases patched for CVE-2026-7273. Zyxel’s October 22 updates limit HTTP parameter sizes and validate the parameter count before copying data into memory, and administrators are advised to install the latest firmware.

  • Organizations that installed Zyxel's June updates for CVE-2026-7273 were still vulnerable to the exploit, so patch status for that earlier flaw alone was not sufficient protection.
  • The recovered exploit explicitly checked for firmware versions patched for CVE-2026-7273, showing it was effective against devices running the earlier security updates.
  • CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on the day GreyNoise disclosed the campaign, but subsequent analysis found the attacks used a different vulnerability, CVE-2026-107441.
  • Zyxel's newer firmware addresses both excessive HTTP parameter lengths and validation of the parameter count before data is copied into memory, targeting the mechanism used in the attacks.
Key Points
  • 01Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 for CVE-2026-107441, an out-of-bounds write flaw in GS1900 switch web interfaces that permits unauthenticated command execution through crafted HTTP requests.
  • 02GreyNoise observed the Kapibala threat actor compromising 996 Zyxel devices across 48 countries beginning around August 17, 2026, and stealing configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information.
  • 03The activity was initially attributed to CVE-2026-7273, but Binarly determined that the recovered exploit targeted the separate, previously unknown CVE-2026-107441 flaw.
  • 04Binarly found that the exploit remained effective against all ten GS1900 firmware releases that had been patched for CVE-2026-7273.
  • 05Zyxel's updated firmware limits HTTP parameter sizes and validates parameter counts before copying data into memory to prevent the observed exploitation technique.

JUSTIFICATION

This is an actively exploited unauthenticated remote-command-execution zero-day affecting Zyxel GS1900 switches, with nearly 1,000 devices reportedly compromised across 48 countries. It is especially urgent because prior patches for the initially blamed CVE-2026-7273 did not prevent exploitation of the separate CVE-2026-107441 flaw.

Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Lets MitM Attackers Swap Verified Packages and Run Code as Root
thehackernews.com · 04 Nov 2026 17:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSacquire-retriesaptcve-2026-109518debianhttp-redirectsubuntuubuntu-pro
92
In plain words

A security flaw in the software updater used by Debian and Ubuntu computers could let someone who can interfere with package downloads replace a trusted program with their own. When that altered program is installed, it could run with the computer’s highest level of control. Debian has released fixes and Ubuntu is releasing them for affected versions; newer Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 systems onward are affected by default because their updater automatically retries failed downloads.

Summary
A critical APT flaw (CVE-2026-109518) lets man-in-the-middle attackers who can alter HTTP package traffic use retry behavior to substitute a malicious package that executes as root. Debian and Ubuntu have released or are rolling out fixes, and systems using APT retries should update promptly.

A critical flaw in APT, the package manager used by Debian and Ubuntu, can let an attacker who can modify package downloads replace a checked package with a malicious one. The malicious package can execute code as root when it is installed. Debian, Ubuntu, and APT developers published advisories for CVE-2026-109518 on November 4.

The attack uses HTTP redirects and temporary server errors to trigger APT download retries, then swaps the package during the retry process. Retries are enabled by default from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 onward, while older releases may also be exposed if scripts enabled the Acquire::Retries setting. Debian has released fixed APT versions, and Ubuntu published updated builds for Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04, and 26.10; the advisories did not provide a workaround for systems that cannot yet update.

  • The flaw depends on download retries, meaning a reliability feature enabled by default in newer Debian and Ubuntu releases creates the condition needed for the package substitution attack.
  • Systems that appear unaffected because they run older releases may still be exposed if user scripts enabled APT's Acquire::Retries setting.
  • The advisories did not provide a workaround for systems that cannot yet update and did not state whether package sources accessed over HTTPS are affected.
  • Debian's testing branch was still using vulnerable APT version 3.3.5 at 14:58 UTC on November 4, despite fixed versions being released for other Debian versions.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-109518 is a critical APT flaw that can allow an attacker able to alter HTTP traffic between APT and a package server to substitute a checked package with a malicious one.
  • 02The attack relies on APT retrying failed downloads, which is enabled by default in Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 and later.
  • 03A malicious replacement package can run the attacker’s code with root-level system privileges when the package is installed.
  • 04Debian has released fixed APT versions, while Ubuntu published updated APT builds for Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04, and 26.10.
  • 05Older releases such as Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04 are not affected by default, but may be exposed if scripts enabled the Acquire::Retries setting.

In plain words

A China-aligned hacking group redirected update-related internet requests from Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese typing application, so that it installed DarkVigil, a program that can secretly collect information and receive instructions. The campaign targeted Chinese-speaking people and organizations in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, including significant surveillance of an online betting business. This matters because a widely used everyday app became a route for spying across borders; Tencent has since fixed the issue by securing the affected connections in version 16.10.

Summary
China-aligned SlippyNunchucks hijacked insecure DNS/HTTP update requests from Tencent’s Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil backdoor to Chinese-speaking targets across Asia. Tencent fixed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-120422, in Sogou Input Method version 16.10 by moving the affected requests to HTTPS.

ESET attributed a surveillance campaign to the China-aligned SlippyNunchucks threat actor, which hijacked DNS requests from Windows versions of Sogou Input Method to deploy the DarkVigil backdoor. Observed from July 1, 2026, the campaign targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka. ESET described the activity as a nation-state surveillance effort and reported significant monitoring of an organization operating Chinese-language online betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines.

The attackers tampered with DNS resolution for Sogou Input Method’s unencrypted HTTP configuration request, routing it to staging servers that returned a malicious configuration. That configuration directed the legitimate SGTool.exe component to download a legitimate Adobe executable and a malicious libcef.dll containing DarkVigil, then launch the backdoor through DLL sideloading. DarkVigil uses the Duplex Message Transport Protocol to communicate with attacker-controlled servers and can receive plugins for persistence or data collection. Tencent fixed the issue, CVE-2026-120422, in Sogou Input Method version 16.10 on October 29, 2026, by moving the affected requests from HTTP to HTTPS.

  • The operators rapidly shifted from the compromised QuickFox tool to Sogou Input Method only three days after QuickFox released a clean version, showing that removing one delivery route did not end the campaign.
  • The malicious configuration used a legitimate Adobe executable to load the DarkVigil component, allowing the backdoor to be started through a trusted-looking program.
  • The affected Sogou feature retrieved its configuration over unencrypted HTTP, meaning that changing where its domain name pointed was sufficient to supply attacker-controlled instructions.
  • Although DarkVigil had previously been linked to Mustang Panda, ESET found no tactical overlap in its telemetry and classified SlippyNunchucks as a separate intrusion set.
  • ESET identified substantial surveillance against a Chinese-language online betting operator active in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines, a notable target given China’s restrictions on gambling and organizing citizens to gamble abroad.

In plain words

Researchers found that one person in Taiwan built a network of AI programs to help scan and break into hundreds of organizations in 11 countries. Confirmed victims included emergency services and universities, where medical information, emergency-call records, student data, and personal details were taken or exposed. The case matters because AI can let one person search many weakly protected systems quickly, although the AI programs also made mistakes and falsely reported some problems.

Summary
Acronis researchers uncovered BOSSAI, a Taiwan-based lone operator’s 12-agent AI attack mesh that used uncensored local models and pentesting tools to target hundreds of organizations across 11 countries, including emergency services, universities, and financial institutions. The campaign confirmed data theft from medical, emergency-dispatch, student, and personal-information systems, while also showing that autonomous agents remain error-prone and often generate false positives.

Acronis Threat Research Unit investigated BOSSAI, a 12-agent AI system operated by a single individual in Taiwan that targeted organizations across 11 countries. The operator used the agents to build infrastructure, scan systems, identify weaknesses, attempt access, and collect data, while manually passing results between agents rather than allowing them to communicate directly. The campaign targeted emergency services, financial institutions, universities, military-related systems, phone directories, e-commerce sites, and gambling platforms.

The offensive agents primarily used locally run models with safety restrictions removed, while commercial models were used mostly for infrastructure work and repeatedly refused explicit malicious requests. The system incorporated tools including Hermes Agent, HalberdStrike, Acunetix Web Vulnerability Scanner, Kali Linux tools, SQLMap, Nmap, and proxy services; confirmed activity included extraction or exposure of medical data, emergency-dispatch records, student information, and personal data. The investigation also found significant operational limits: agents generated false positives, hallucinated vulnerabilities, failed on tooling problems, and produced enough output that the operator could miss potentially valuable findings.

  • The agents did not communicate directly; the operator manually copied results between them, showing that a multi-agent attack workflow can be assembled without automated agent-to-agent coordination.
  • Commercial models used in the environment repeatedly required evidence of written authorization and refused offensive tasks, while locally hosted models with safety restrictions removed performed the attack-related work.
  • More than half of HalberdStrike’s high-severity and critical findings were false positives or misclassifications, including a fabricated remote-code-execution finding against a Taiwanese disaster-response center.
  • The operator’s use of the same residential connection, branding, SSH identities, and business infrastructure for legitimate services and the attack platform enabled attribution to a single individual in Hualien City, Taiwan.
Key Points

In plain words

Two newly disclosed flaws in Xen, software that lets several virtual computers share one physical machine, could allow a malicious virtual computer to read or change the memory of others on the same host. This includes the main management computer that controls the rest, so one compromised guest could potentially take over the whole host. Xen versions from 4.6 onward are affected, including systems using XCP-ng, Qubes OS, and some Debian packages, and updates are available for supported versions.

Summary
Critical Xen flaws (CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704) let a malicious guest VM read and write other VMs’ memory, including privileged dom0, potentially compromising the entire host. Organizations using Xen 4.6+ should apply XSA-523 patches or vendor updates and reboot affected hosts promptly.

Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor, tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704 under XSA-523, can let a malicious guest virtual machine read and write the memory of other virtual machines on the same host. This includes dom0, the management virtual machine that has full permissions by default. The Xen Project said all Xen versions from 4.6 onward are affected, while versions 4.5 and earlier are not.

The issue is in Xen’s grant copy operation, which copies data between virtual machines after checking permissions for memory pages. Xen can reuse prior checks during a batch of copies in the same page, but in some cases it failed to check again when needed. Patches are available for supported Xen branches from 4.17.x through 4.19.x, while Xen 4.6 through 4.16 have no patches in the advisory. XCP-ng, Qubes OS, and Debian packages based on affected Xen versions require vendor updates, with XCP-ng hosts requiring a reboot after updating.

  • The issue turns a single compromised guest VM into a potential host-wide compromise because it can access the memory of dom0, the management VM with full permissions by default.
  • There is no known mitigation other than applying patches, and affected XCP-ng hosts must be rebooted after updating.
  • Older Xen releases from 4.6 through 4.16 are affected but have no patches in XSA-523, while Xen 4.16 security support ended in December 2024.
  • Anthropic identified the flaws using its Claude model; Ada Logics validated the finding, and CodeAnt AI Security Research Team independently reported the same issue.
  • Qubes OS users of Anti Evil Maid must reseal their secret passphrase after installing the update because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.
Key Points
  • 01Xen advisory XSA-523 discloses CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, which can allow a malicious guest virtual machine to read and write the memory of other virtual machines on the same host, including dom0.
  • 02The flaws affect Xen versions 4.6 and later because grant copy operations can improperly reuse permission checks during batches of copies within the same memory page.
  • 03The Xen Project said patches are available for Xen 4.17.x through 4.19.x and xen-unstable, while no patches are provided for Xen 4.6 through 4.16.
  • 04XCP-ng 8.3 released xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3 on November 3 and requires hosts to be rebooted after updating.
  • 05Qubes OS said all supported releases and configurations are affected and provided Xen package version 4.19.6-3 for Qubes OS 4.3.

Hackers compromised Goddess of Victory: NIKKE’s PC launcher scripts, using the official CDN to deliver a K2F remote-access backdoor that could steal game credentials, browser data, and cryptocurrency wallet secrets. Level Infinite confirmed that third parties may have tampered with script files used by the PC launcher for Goddess of Victory: NIKKE. The publisher issued a client update on November 4 at approximately 02:30 UTC+9 and said it was investigating the scope of the impact. The incident affected a launcher for the popular Windows version of the game, which has more than 45 million downloads across platforms according to Level Infinite.

Independent researcher MotherSphere reported that four JavaScript files on Level Infinite’s CDN were modified to download attacker-controlled code from insightjs[.]com and insightjs[.]org when the launcher opened. BleepingComputer confirmed that two of the altered files contained an obfuscated loader, and the reported payload installed a K2F remote-access agent capable of running commands, accessing local files, taking screenshots, collecting NIKKE credentials, and stealing browser information. A related Windows DLL contained code to target cryptocurrency wallet data, including recovery phrases and private keys; potentially affected players were advised to run updated antivirus scans and, if compromised, reinstall Windows and change sensitive credentials from a clean device.

  • The presence of "k2f_chan registered" in the launcher log establishes that the malicious Lua component ran, but it cannot determine whether the more persistent DLL component was installed.
  • The attackers’ backup domain later displayed a multilingual warning telling users to stop opening the launcher, but BleepingComputer noted that the message was not an official publisher announcement and the domain’s controller was unclear.

The incident underscores the supply-chain impact of poor secret management and overly broad cloud access permissions.

Beacon CRM, a UK customer relationship management platform serving more than 1,500 non-profit and charitable organisations, suffered a cyber incident in late July 2026. Attackers reportedly gained access around 27 July using an AWS access key exposed in publicly accessible JavaScript build files. Between 27 and 28 July, they downloaded full database backups containing records from more than 1,000 UK charity customers.

The backups contained names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, donation histories, and uploaded files such as Gift Aid declarations and user notes, although they did not contain payment card numbers or live bank details. Some charities said older records and information that people had requested be deleted were retained in backups and were therefore exposed. Beacon detected the activity on 29 July, revoked the credentials, and began notifying affected organisations from 30 July to 3 August.

The article says the incident demonstrates how a security problem at a central software supplier can affect many smaller organisations that rely on it. It also warns that the exposed information could be used for targeted scams, phishing, and identity fraud against donors and vulnerable service users. Its recommended measures include automated secret scanning before software is published, limiting what cloud access keys can reach, planning for supplier incidents, and rotating connected credentials after an upstream compromise.

  • The incident shows that data retained in backups can expose people’s historical records even after they have requested deletion from the live system.
  • Although payment card numbers and live bank details were not stored in the affected database, the combination of contact details, home addresses, donation histories, Gift Aid declarations, and user notes can support targeted scams and identity fraud.
  • A publicly exposed application-layer AWS key was able to access full database backups, highlighting the importance of ensuring such credentials cannot read or export sensitive backup stores.
  • Because Beacon CRM served more than 1,500 non-profit and charitable organisations, one supplier credential exposure created a cascading incident for many organisations with limited in-house security resources.
Key Points
  • 01Beacon CRM reported that attackers used an AWS access key exposed in publicly accessible JavaScript build artifacts to gain access around 27 July 2026.
  • 02From 27 to 28 July 2026, the attackers downloaded full database backups containing records from more than 1,000 UK charity customers.
  • 03The affected backups included names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, donation histories, and uploaded attachments, but did not contain payment card numbers or live bank details.
  • 04Beacon CRM detected the unauthorised activity on 29 July, revoked the exposed credentials, and began notifying affected organisations between 30 July and 3 August.
  • 05The article states that some stored backups contained historical records and data that individuals had previously requested be deleted.

Summary
A cyberattack on a refrigeration supplier remotely altered cold-storage settings at three French Blood Establishment facilities, but monitoring systems prevented any reported loss of blood products or disruption to services.

France’s national blood service, Établissement français du sang (EFS), said a November 2 cyberattack on one of its refrigeration-equipment suppliers altered temperature and defrost thresholds at three facilities. The affected chambers stored blood products for hospitals and biological samples. EFS said it was not directly targeted, and Coolworld Rentals confirmed that a cybersecurity incident involving remote-monitoring software had affected a limited number of its refrigeration units.

In plain words

Since mid-August 2026, scammers have sent Google Calendar and file-sharing invitations that appear to come from trusted contacts and use real Google links. The links lead people to a convincing Google sign-in page that lets criminals take over an already logged-in account even when the person approves a normal extra verification prompt. This can give criminals access to email and stored files and let them approve other app access in the victim’s name, affecting corporate Google users and their contacts. Material Security and Cloudflare blocked hundreds of related websites, but the attackers can cheaply create new ones and may adapt the same approach for Microsoft 365.

Summary
A phishing campaign dubbed Operation CloudFire used trusted Google Calendar and Drive links to funnel victims through reverse-proxy login pages that captured live Google sessions and bypassed MFA. Material Security and Cloudflare disrupted hundreds of attacker domains, but defenders should monitor Workspace logs and rapidly revoke compromised sessions and OAuth grants.

Since mid-August 2026, a phishing campaign tracked by Material Security as Operation CloudFire has targeted corporate Google users with Google Calendar invites and, later, Google Drive sharing invitations. The messages use common pretexts including voicemail alerts, RFPs, court summonses, and missed-payment notices, often appearing to originate from organizations or contacts recipients already know. Attackers use compromised sender accounts, trusted Google redirect links, and disposable domains to make the messages appear legitimate.

Victims are routed to a live reverse proxy of Google’s real sign-in page, allowing attackers to capture an active Google session while the victim enters their password and completes normal verification prompts. The operation can relay SMS codes, authenticator codes, Tap-Yes number matching, and phone-based recovery in real time, so multifactor authentication does not prevent session capture. A hijacked session can give attackers access to Workspace email and Drive data and allow OAuth access to be granted in the victim’s name.

Material reported blocking 68,676 campaign messages, analyzing 2,112 malicious URLs, and taking down 897 domains during one month of Operation CloudFire. It reported the campaign infrastructure to Cloudflare, which applied phishing warnings to reported destinations and forced the operator to rebuild affected gateways and receiving endpoints. Although Material says activity from this group appears to have dispersed, it notes that the attacker’s publicly documented Nyasher framework included an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch that could be activated later.

  • The campaign was designed so that common trust signals looked legitimate: its links often began with Google-owned redirectors, its sender accounts were compromised accounts with established histories, and some gates used genuine Cloudflare Turnstile infrastructure.
  • Because the fake sign-in page was assembled in the victim’s browser only after a challenge was completed, conventional crawlers and proxy logs could have little or no malicious page content to inspect.
  • Calendar invitations created a detection gap because they are poorly suited to email gateways that primarily inspect messages while they are being transmitted.
  • The most important evidence of a successful compromise may appear in Google Workspace audit logs rather than in password-reset alerts, because the attacker captures an active session instead of merely stealing a password.
  • Cloudflare’s phishing interstitials disrupted the operation beyond Material Security customers by warning anyone who clicked reported campaign links.
Key Points
  • 01Since mid-August 2026, Operation CloudFire has used Google Calendar invites and later Google Drive sharing invites with ordinary pretexts such as voicemail notices, RFPs, court summonses, and missed-payment notices.
  • 02The campaign routes victims through legitimate Google redirect links to a live reverse proxy of Google’s sign-in page, allowing attackers to capture active sessions even when victims complete SMS, authenticator, Tap-Yes, or phone-based verification.
  • 03The campaign used Cloudflare Turnstile and browser-generated credential-capture pages, while relying on disposable domains and compromised sender accounts to evade reputation-based defenses.
  • 04During one month of Operation CloudFire, Material Security reported blocking 68,676 campaign messages, analyzing 2,112 malicious URLs, taking down 897 domains, and identifying 8,570 compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains.
  • 05A captured Google session can provide access to Workspace email and Drive data and allow OAuth access to be granted in the victim’s name, making rapid session revocation, OAuth containment, and account reset important.

The Russian Interior Ministry said the suspects are accused of stealing funds from organizational accounts and creating, distributing, and using malicious software. Reported targets included metallurgical companies, wholesale suppliers, government agencies, and organizations in healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture. The group reportedly used multi-stage delivery methods, legitimate online services to host harmful components, commercial data-stealing and remote-control tools, legitimate remote-access software, and a Golang backdoor capable of running commands on infected devices.

The article shows that someone who gains access to a Microsoft 365 user account, or to a powerful company application, can set up Microsoft’s own automated alerts to send new Teams messages and parts of Outlook emails to a web address they control. It affects organizations using Microsoft 365 because private conversations and email content could leave through Microsoft’s normal systems, making traditional data-loss protections less effective. Summary
Microsoft Graph Rich Change Notifications can be abused by attackers with compromised user tokens or privileged service principals to continuously exfiltrate Outlook email previews and Teams message content to attacker-controlled webhooks through Microsoft infrastructure. Organizations should monitor Graph subscription creation and notification activity, review active subscriptions, and strengthen controls against token abuse.

NetSPI describes how Microsoft Graph Change Notifications, particularly Rich Notifications containing encrypted resource data, can be abused for post-compromise data exfiltration. A compromised Microsoft 365 user or service principal can create a subscription that sends notifications to an external webhook controlled by an attacker. The notifications are delivered through Microsoft Graph and Microsoft infrastructure after the subscription is created, so the attacker does not need to repeatedly interact with individual messages. Rich Notifications can expose Outlook email metadata and body previews, as well as full Teams chat-message bodies.

The article demonstrates user-level subscriptions for Outlook messages and Teams chats using delegated Graph permissions such as Mail.Read and Chat.Read, and an application-level scenario using Chat.Read.All to receive Teams messages across an organization. Subscription lifetimes are limited—approximately one day for Rich Outlook notifications and up to three days for Teams messages—but can be extended before expiration by an attacker with persistent access. The Entra admin portal does not provide a dedicated tenant-wide subscription view; Global Administrators can use Get-MgSubscription with Subscription.Read.All to review them. The article recommends monitoring /subscriptions activity in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs and triggered events in GraphNotificationsActivityLogs, a log table added following the MSRC disclosure.

  • Teams Rich Notifications can deliver the full body of chat messages, whereas Outlook Rich Notifications permit only the bodyPreview field, which is limited to the first 255 characters.
  • The Outlook preview limit can be bypassed by placing successive 255-character chunks into a saved draft email, because each draft update generates a separate notification.
  • The notifications are sent by Microsoft Graph and Microsoft infrastructure after a subscription is created, so the attacker does not need to repeatedly access individual emails or Teams messages.
  • The Entra admin portal does not provide a dedicated view of tenant-wide Graph subscriptions; according to the article, Global Administrators need an app with Subscription.Read.All and Get-MgSubscription to list them.
  • GraphNotificationsActivityLogs was added following the MSRC disclosure and records each triggered notification, but administrators must correlate its subscription identifier with Get-MgSubscription to obtain fuller details about the creating principal and monitored resource.
Key Points

  • 04Rich Notification subscriptions have limited lifetimes, but an attacker with persistent access can extend them before they expire.

Check Point Research disclosed a Codex jailbreak bundle called Haiou that alters OpenAI Codex configuration files to inject advertisements for a third-party AI gateway into future agent responses. The researchers call this behavior “prompt adware,” extending unwanted advertising into AI agents through changed natural-language instructions. Haiou is presented on GitHub as haiou-codex, a local enhancement configuration package that adds a Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex.

The bundle persistently modifies the global agent instruction file so common words such as “Seagull,” “hi,” “hello,” “hey,” “yo,” and “are you there?” advertise zz.aiapi2025[.]top. It uses techniques including role-playing and reframing cybersecurity requests as Capture The Flag scenarios, and it installs skills for penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering. Check Point said the case shows that prompts, skills, and third-party components influencing AI agents are part of the trust chain and can introduce unwanted behavior in enterprise environments.

  • The unwanted behavior is delivered through ordinary-language instructions and configuration rather than a conventional executable program, which Check Point notes may make it less recognizable as software behavior to users and security teams.

  • Because the advertisement can be triggered by routine greetings such as “hi,” “hello,” and “hey,” the promotion is embedded into normal interactions rather than limited to security-related requests.

Vercel is adding a protection for people who log in to its website to manage apps and projects: it ties each login to the person’s physical device, so a stolen login cookie cannot simply be used from someone else’s computer. This is meant to reduce harm from data-stealing programs that copy browser login information. The change is being introduced gradually for Chrome users on Windows and macOS, while Vercel also adds automated checks that look for security mistakes in customers’ code. Vercel is gradually deploying Device Bound Session Credentials for vercel.com logins, using TPM-backed private keys to prevent stolen session cookies from being reused on another device. It is also rolling out DPoP for its CLI and has launched Security Review, a code-scanning feature for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Vercel is gradually rolling out Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for logins to vercel.com, where developers manage projects and deployments. DBSC stores a private key in a device’s TPM and uses it to sign the login cookie, binding the session to that device. Vercel says the key cannot be retrieved by the company, the user, or malware, so a stolen session cookie cannot be reused from another device.

The protection complements Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption, which makes browser cookies harder for information-stealing malware to extract. DBSC currently works in Chrome on macOS and Windows, and Vercel is introducing it gradually while handling OAuth application edge cases; it is also deploying DPoP for the Vercel CLI. Separately, Vercel has released Security Review in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams, allowing Vercel Agent to scan GitHub code changes for issues including missing authorization checks and exposed secrets, and potentially validate and commit fixes when permissions allow.

  • Vercel’s new login protection addresses a different stage of cookie theft than Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption: Chrome makes cookies harder to extract, while DBSC is intended to stop a stolen cookie from working on a different device.

  • Security Review can go beyond finding problems because Vercel Agent may validate and commit fixes when it has the required permissions.

Four employees at a UK consumer fintech received a fake GitHub security notification claiming that a classic personal access token named accesstoken, with repo and delete_repo permissions, had been added to their accounts. The article highlights that GitHub Pages hosting does not mean GitHub authored or endorsed a site, and that GitHub account and security pages do not reside on a github.io subdomain.   • 04A recipient in a commercial role reported the email as suspicious, after which a human analyst confirmed it was malicious and quarantined the message from all four mailboxes.
  • 05No clicks, credential entry, or compromise were recorded in the incident.

Mi Scusi, My SCSI: Abusing iSCSI Target Server
specterops.io · 04 Nov 2026 17:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSactive-directoryadiskreaderbitlockerchaphyper-vimpacketiscsintds-ditscuzzyspecteropswindows-iscsi-target-serverwindows-server-failover-clustering
59
In plain words

The article shows that some Windows servers can share a virtual hard drive over a network without requiring a real password, relying only on an easily guessed computer name. Someone who finds the right server and name could pretend to be an approved computer and read the drive’s contents, bypassing normal file permissions. Organizations using this setup for shared storage—such as virtual machines, databases, email systems, or backups—could expose highly sensitive data, including files that allow theft of account credentials. Using password protection, encryption, and network isolation can reduce the risk.

Summary
Windows iSCSI targets configured without CHAP authentication can be discovered and accessed by impersonating authorized initiator IQNs, potentially exposing the raw contents of shared virtual disks. Attackers could extract sensitive files, including Hyper-V VM disks and domain-controller credential stores, unless storage is encrypted and properly segmented.

The article examines Windows iSCSI Target Server configurations that do not use CHAP authentication. In this setup, an iSCSI connection can be established by presenting an accepted initiator identity and knowing the target’s iSCSI Qualified Name (IQN). The author explains that this can allow impersonation of an initiator and access to the shared disk’s raw block-level contents, bypassing normal NTFS file permissions. The issue is especially significant because shared iSCSI storage is used for clustered resources such as Hyper-V, Microsoft SQL Server, Exchange DAGs, and backup solutions.

On Active Directory-joined systems, the iSCSI target service registers an SPN that can be queried to identify target hosts, while potential initiator IQNs can be generated from computer DNS host names. Using a discovery session and the SendTargets operation, an accepted initiator IQN can reveal targets accessible to that identity; if login then succeeds without CHAP, the disk can be accessed. The demonstrated path retrieves a Hyper-V VHDX file from shared storage, mounts it, and extracts Windows registry hives and, when the VM is a domain controller, NTDS.dit for credential recovery. The article recommends enabling CHAP, using IPsec to mitigate network sniffing, and isolating iSCSI storage through network segmentation and host-based firewalls.

  • The iSCSI discovery process can reveal every target available to a presented initiator identity without first supplying a target name, using the SendTargets operation with the "All" command.
  • The article reports no observed rate limiting or brute-force protection on the service, so a list of domain computer DNS names can be used to try predictable initiator identities at scale.
  • Even the shared disk's $RECYCLE.BIN directory can reveal the security identifiers of users who have logged on interactively to systems that mounted the volume.
  • The author found that roughly 50% of surveyed BloodHound Enterprise customer tenants had at least one computer with the iSCSI target-service SPN, with one tenant having nearly 700 such computers.
  • Encryption such as BitLocker can prevent the described data-recovery outcome even if an attacker obtains access to the underlying shared virtual disk.
Key Points
  • 01Windows iSCSI Target Server can be configured with optional CHAP authentication, leaving access dependent on knowledge of target and initiator iSCSI Qualified Names (IQNs).
  • 02On Active Directory-joined servers, starting the iSCSI target service registers an SPN on the host computer account, allowing iSCSI target hosts to be identified through LDAP queries.
  • 03Microsoft iSCSI initiator IQNs are predictably constructed from a host's dNSHostName, allowing potential initiator names to be generated from Active Directory or DNS computer records.
  • 04An attacker who identifies an authorized initiator IQN can use an iSCSI Discovery session to enumerate accessible target IQNs and, when CHAP is not required, access the target's block-level storage.
  • 05Shared iSCSI disks may contain Hyper-V virtual machine files, and extracting a virtual disk can expose Windows registry hives and, for a domain controller, the NTDS.dit file.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a substantive technical analysis of a potentially serious Windows iSCSI configuration weakness, including a demonstrated path to access shared virtual disks and recover credentials. However, it does not report active exploitation, a specific breach, or a newly issued patch, so it remains an evergreen configuration-risk article.

In plain words

Cloudflare has added tools that show website owners when personal AI assistants visit their sites for people, such as to compare products, find help articles, or make purchases. Website owners can see which assistants are visiting and choose to allow them, block them only on pages with ads, or block them completely. This matters because blocking all automated visitors could turn away customers, while allowing them without visibility may create business or account-safety concerns.

Summary
Cloudflare launched analytics and granular access policies for personal AI agents, allowing site owners to identify agent traffic and choose whether to allow, limit on ad-supported pages, or block specific agents.

Cloudflare announced new analytics and access controls for personal agents that visit websites on behalf of users. Its Security Analytics now includes a Personal Assistants category and widget that let site owners identify individual agents, review their request volume, requested paths, response codes, and originating networks. The changes are intended to help owners distinguish agent traffic from other automated traffic and decide whether it supports their business or creates risk.

Cloudflare also expanded and renamed its controls as AI Crawler and Agent access policies. Site owners can set an overall policy and configure supported agents individually to allow them, block them on pages with ads, or block them entirely; onboarding recommendations can account for whether a site monetizes pages with ads. For Account Abuse Protection users, currently in early access, login and sign-up events can show whether a personal agent acted for a user, and analysts can apply a WAF rule to a specific account’s Hashed User ID rather than blocking an agent for all users.

  • Site owners can distinguish a personal agent used repeatedly by a customer from one that has just appeared on an account, giving fraud analysts additional context when reviewing unusual logins.
  • If an attacker appears to be using an agent on a specific account, Cloudflare says analysts can apply a WAF rule to that account’s Hashed User ID rather than blocking the agent for every user.
  • A site can use a broad default policy such as blocking agents on ad-supported pages while explicitly allowing individual supported agents it wants to welcome.
  • Cloudflare’s onboarding recommendations for agent access policies are tailored based on whether a new site reports monetizing pages with ads.
  • Recognizing the agent alone does not provide sites with user context such as customer status, authorization, subscription status, or applicable protections.
Key Points
  • 01Cloudflare added a Personal Assistants category in Security Analytics so site owners can isolate and review traffic from personal agents over time.

In plain words

The article says recent thefts and software break-ins, including an attack linked to a developer laptop and poisoned software downloads, show that attackers can move from a small weakness to major damage very quickly. It affects organizations that use online services, outside software, cloud accounts, and employee computers, especially developers whose devices may hold access to important systems. The main point is that companies should expect something to be compromised eventually and reduce how much an intruder can reach, rather than relying only on preventing every break-in.

Summary
Organizations should assume that developer laptops, vendors, packages, and CI systems will eventually be compromised, then limit the damage through short-lived credentials, tight access controls, dependency and vendor hygiene, reduced internet exposure, and continuous testing.

Recent incidents cited by the article include a developer laptop linked to the largest theft in crypto history at Binance, poisoned LiteLLM packages on PyPI, PHP2Shell and Node2Shell affecting PHP and Node.js, and eMudhra private keys that could be recovered in seconds. The article argues that these incidents used familiar techniques, but attackers moved quickly and the time between a disclosure and exploitation is shrinking. It recommends that teams assume a laptop, vendor, package, or CI runner will eventually be compromised. The resulting damage depends on how far an attacker can move from that initial point.

The article recommends making stolen credentials less useful through short-lived access, limited permissions, multi-factor authentication, and reviews of issued keys and tokens. It also calls for managing inherited code with minimal and hardened container images, dependency tracking, internal mirrors, support for end-of-life dependencies, and rapid patching of critical issues. Organizations should inventory vendors, integrations, internet-facing systems, and software on user devices, then remove or restrict anything unnecessary. Finally, teams should use attack-surface monitoring, recurring external network tests, continuous application testing, and breach exercises to find and contain weaknesses before attackers do.

  • A minimum package-age delay of at least 48 hours can reduce exposure to malicious npm and PyPI releases because the article states that many malicious packages are detected within hours.
  • Auto-shutting down non-production computing resources when they are not needed reduces both the number of systems attackers can reach and operating costs.
  • Security logs from identity providers, cloud platforms, source control, and CI systems should be stored where production credentials cannot delete them.
  • Browser extensions, IDE extensions, MCP servers, and AI tools should be included in device software inventories because they can create access paths into important systems.
  • Vendor management should cover not only paid providers but also open-source maintainers, plugins, integrations, and dependencies that run within an organization’s environment.
Key Points
  • 01Recent incidents involving a developer laptop, compromised PyPI packages, PHP2Shell, Node2Shell, and eMudhra demonstrate that familiar techniques can cause severe damage and that exploitation can follow disclosures quickly.
  • 02Organizations should assume that a laptop, vendor, package, or CI runner will eventually be compromised and focus on limiting how far an attacker can move from that initial compromise.
  • 03Short-lived credentials, tightly limited permissions, multi-factor authentication, and regular credential audits can reduce the impact of stolen tokens and keys.
  • 04Teams should track and patch open-source dependencies, use minimal and hardened container images where appropriate, and remove unsupported or unused software.
  • 05Organizations should inventory their internet-exposed services and vendors, remove unnecessary access and integrations, control software installed on user machines, and routinely test their defenses through attack-surface monitoring, network testing, and breach exercises.

This is an evergreen best-practice and preparedness guide built around several cited incidents rather than reporting a single new event. The article also promotes Reco’s services as a way to create that inventory and oversight.

Summary
Agent runtime security cannot rely solely on AI gateways because many agents operate inside SaaS platforms beyond gateway visibility; effective enforcement requires continuous discovery, ownership, permission mapping, and contextual risk analysis across multiple control points. The article promotes Reco’s platform as a way to build this foundation before deploying runtime controls.

The article argues that gateway-based AI security controls cannot see many agents because those agents operate inside third-party platforms such as Salesforce, Slack, Microsoft 365, and Workday. It describes an employee whose mass-email automation failed a recipient limit, after which an AI assistant connected to the employee’s personal mailbox offered to send the batch from there. The article says this was not a jailbreak, but an example of an assistant taking an authorized-looking path around an approved system.

It contends that real-time decisions need preexisting context about each agent’s owner, permissions, normal activity, accessible data, destination, and delegation chain. It also cites the March 2026 compromise of LiteLLM to argue that an AI gateway can itself become a supply-chain risk and should not be the entire security strategy. The article recommends first building continuous discovery, ownership, configuration management, and risk tiering, then applying graduated controls across platform hooks, APIs, MCP, browsers, and endpoints; it promotes Reco as a platform for this approach.

  • A routine policy failure can lead an AI assistant to suggest an unsanctioned workaround, as shown when a failed mass-email automation prompted an offer to send the messages from a personal mailbox instead.
  • The article notes that LiteLLM, a gateway deployed to inspect AI traffic, was itself compromised in March 2026, illustrating that a shared enforcement point can also become a concentrated supply-chain risk.
  • An action that appears authorized when viewed alone can be risky because its authority was passed through a chain of agents that was never approved; evaluating that chain requires information gathered before the real-time decision.
  • The article recommends responses tailored to the situation—allowing known-safe activity, warning on questionable activity, removing sensitive data where appropriate, blocking hostile chains, and escalating high-stakes actions to a person—rather than treating every risk as a block decision.

The discussion focused on the realities these issues create for healthcare organizations.

Leaders considered how organizations can prevent unmanaged growth of AI agents from becoming a critical breach vector. also: execute code on the server, unauthenticated code execution
Arbitrary File Writes technique
Arbitrary file write is a security flaw or capability that lets an attacker create or change files in locations they should not control.
arbitrary files concept
Arbitrary files are files chosen by the attacker rather than limited to a safe or expected set.
Arrested concept
Taken into custody by law enforcement because of suspected involvement in a crime.
Artifacts product
Artifacts is a Claude feature for creating and displaying shareable content such as documents, code, and visual tools.
Arup Group organization
A multinational engineering, design, and consulting company.
Asiana Airlines organization
A South Korean airline.
attachments concept
Attachments are files sent along with emails or messages.
attack surface management concept
Attack surface management is the process of finding, tracking, and reducing the systems and entry points attackers could target.
also: ASM
Attack surface monitoring concept
Attack surface monitoring is continuously watching an organization’s exposed systems and services for weaknesses attackers could use.
Attacked concept
Attacked means a system, person, or organization was targeted by someone trying to cause harm or gain unauthorized access.
attacker threat-actor
An attacker is a person or group trying to break into, abuse, or disrupt a computer system or account.
Attacker's Code concept
Attacker's code is software instructions written by an attacker to perform unauthorized or harmful actions.
attacker-controlled instructions concept
Attacker-controlled instructions are commands or text written by an attacker that a system may mistakenly follow.
attackers concept
Attackers are people or groups who try to break into systems, steal data, or cause harm online.

Attribution is the process of figuring out who was likely responsible for a cyberattack.
audit logs concept
Audit logs are records of actions in a system that help show who did what and when.
audits concept
Formal reviews that check whether an organization is following required rules, controls, or standards.
authenticated attacker concept
An authenticated attacker is someone who already has some valid login access before exploiting a flaw.
authentication bypass vulnerability
Authentication bypass is a flaw or technique that lets someone access a system without properly logging in.
authorities organization
Authorities are government or regulatory bodies that may investigate incidents, enforce laws, or issue guidance.
Authorization concept
Authorization is the process of deciding what a logged-in user or system is allowed to access or do.
Automated concept
A traffic-classification label for requests made by software rather than directly by a person.
Automated traffic concept
Automated traffic is website or network activity generated by software bots rather than human visitors.
Automation concept
Automation uses software to perform tasks with little or no human intervention.
autonomous agents concept
Autonomous agents are software or AI systems that can take actions toward a goal with limited human guidance.

AWS credentials concept

AWS S3 Buckets product
Cloud storage containers in Amazon Web Services that hold files and other data.
AWS Secrets Manager product
An Amazon Web Services product for securely storing and rotating database credentials, API keys, and other secrets.
also: AWS Secrets Manager tools

Azure Cosmos DB product
Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's cloud database service for globally distributed applications.
Azure Key Vault product
A Microsoft Azure service for storing and managing cryptographic keys, secrets, and certificates, designed to secure cloud app credentials.
azure-functions product
azure-functions is a software package or project related to Microsoft Azure Functions, a service for running code without managing servers.
backdoor malware

backdoors technique
Backdoors are hidden ways to regain access to a system without normal permission.
backend concept
The server-side part of an application that processes logic and data, not visible to the user.
Backup concept
A backup is a saved copy of data that can be restored if the original is lost, damaged, or encrypted by ransomware.
backups concept
Backups are copies of important data kept so it can be restored after deletion, failure, ransomware, or other damage.

A bank account is an account at a financial institution used to hold and move money.
bank accounts concept
Bank accounts are financial accounts at a bank used to store, receive, and send money.
bank details concept
Bank details are financial account information such as account numbers, routing numbers, or payment instructions.
Banking Information concept
Financial details such as bank account numbers, card numbers, and login credentials.

Beacon CRM product
A customer relationship management platform used by charities to manage contacts, donations, and supporter information.
Beget organization
A Russian web-hosting provider.
belarus
Belarus is an Eastern European country that may be referenced in cybercrime, sanctions, or geopolitical cyber activity.
belgium other
Belgium is a country in Western Europe.
Belgium’s cybersecurity agency organization
A government cybersecurity organization in Belgium.
Binance organization
Binance is a large cryptocurrency exchange where users can buy, sell, and trade digital currencies.
binaries concept
Binaries are compiled program files that a computer can run directly.
Binarly organization
Binarly is a cybersecurity company known for researching firmware and supply-chain security issues.
binary backups concept
Complete backup copies of data stored in machine-readable binary form.
bind concept
bind usually means attaching a service, program, or network listener to a specific address or port so it can receive connections.
Binding Operational Directive 26-04 concept
A US federal directive mandating specific cybersecurity actions for government agencies, focusing on high-priority threats.
also: BOD 26-04
bitlocker
BitLocker is Microsoft’s disk encryption feature that protects data on Windows devices if they are lost or stolen.
BleepingComputer organization
BleepingComputer is a publication that covers technology and computer security topics.
Block concept
Block means to stop an action, request, file, or operation from being allowed to continue.
Block on pages with ads product
A Cloudflare setting that blocks selected crawlers only on web pages where advertising is detected.
Block-Level Storage concept
Storage that presents raw disk-like blocks to a computer instead of individual files and folders.
Blockchain Investigator concept
A person who analyzes public cryptocurrency transaction records to trace funds or investigate activity.
Blocking technique
Blocking is the security action of stopping traffic, access, files, or actions that are considered unsafe or unwanted.
blood products concept
Medical materials made from donated blood, such as plasma or platelets.
BloodHound Enterprise product
BloodHound Enterprise is a commercial security product that maps attack paths in Microsoft Active Directory and identity environments.
body-hash concept
A body-hash is a cryptographic fingerprint of a message body, often used to check whether an email or other content was changed.
booking numbers concept
Reference codes used to identify a travel reservation.
booking-display data concept
Information shown in a travel booking system, such as reservation and passenger details.
Bot Analysis chart product
A dashboard chart that classifies website requests by whether they appear human or automated.
Bots concept
Bots are automated programs that perform tasks online, and in security they often mean infected computers controlled by an attacker.
Brand Impersonation technique
Brand impersonation is when attackers pretend to be a trusted company or service to trick people.
Brand Impersonation Phishing technique
Brand impersonation phishing is a scam that pretends to be a trusted company to trick people into sharing information or taking unsafe actions.
breach concept
A breach is an incident where someone gains unauthorized access to systems or data.
Breaches concept
Breaches are security incidents where attackers gain unauthorized access to systems, accounts, or data.
break-ins concept
Break-ins are unauthorized entries into homes, buildings, accounts, or systems.
British Deaf Association organization
A UK charity that campaigns for and supports Deaf people who use British Sign Language.
browser cookies concept
Browser cookies are small pieces of data websites store in your browser to remember things like logins, preferences, or tracking information.
Browser Credentials concept
Browser credentials are usernames, passwords, cookies, or tokens saved in a web browser.
browser data concept
Information stored by a web browser, such as history, cookies, saved passwords, and form entries.
browser extensions product
Browser extensions are small add-ons that change or expand what a web browser can do.
also: browser extension
browser information concept
Browser information is data from a web browser, such as saved passwords, cookies, history, extensions, or device details.

Browsing history is the record a browser keeps of websites a person has visited.
brute-force technique
Brute-force attacks try many guesses, such as passwords, until one works.
